sections.heading: What is sildenafil used for?
sections.body:
Sildenafil is a medicine used to treat erection problems, also called erectile dysfunction. The NHS says it is also sometimes used for pulmonary hypertension, which is high blood pressure in the blood vessels that supply the lungs. Most men aged 18 and over can use it for erection problems. Most adults and children aged 1 year and over can use it for pulmonary hypertension. Brand names for the erection use include Viagra, Aronix, Liberize and Nipatra.

The NHS says women can take sildenafil for pulmonary hypertension, but there is no good evidence that it helps sexual problems in women. A hospital leaflet describes sildenafil as a second-line treatment for Raynaud's phenomenon and for digital ulcers. Local NHS prescribing guidance says generic sildenafil can be prescribed on the NHS where clinically appropriate, while branded Viagra is limited to men who meet set criteria. Private prescriptions are an option for people who do not qualify. The MHRA has reclassified Viagra Connect tablets as a pharmacy medicine.

sections.heading: How does sildenafil work?
sections.body:
Sildenafil belongs to a group of medicines called PDE5 inhibitors. StatPearls says these medicines stop the PDE5 enzyme from breaking down a chemical messenger called cGMP. For erection problems, the NHS says sildenafil temporarily increases blood flow to the penis when a person is sexually aroused. Taken alone it does not cause an erection. In pulmonary hypertension, it relaxes blood vessels in the chest. The NHS says it does not affect any type of contraception, including the combined pill and emergency contraception.

If it does not seem to work, the NHS lists the timing of the dose or a lack of sexual arousal as possible reasons. Other options the NHS lists for erection problems include a vacuum pump, psychological treatments, penile implants and pelvic floor exercises. The NHS also lists losing weight, stopping smoking, a healthy diet, regular exercise and reducing stress and anxiety as steps that can help.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of sildenafil?
sections.body:
Common side effects include headache, indigestion, dizziness and a blocked nose. Many people have no side effects or only mild ones. The NHS says serious side effects are rare. The NHS says the medicine can be taken for a long time, with no lasting harmful effects seen over many months or years.

A painful erection that lasts a long time is listed as a serious side effect, and the advice is to call 999 or go to A&E. For suspected anaphylaxis, a heart attack or a seizure, the NHS gives 999. For a sudden decrease or loss of vision, the NHS says to stop taking sildenafil and call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away. MedlinePlus says the vision loss was permanent in some cases. MedlinePlus also advises calling a doctor right away for a sudden decrease or loss of hearing.

sections.heading: Taking sildenafil with other medicines, drugs and alcohol
sections.body:
The NHS says it can be dangerous to take sildenafil with nitrates, which are often given for chest pain. The combination can cause a dangerous fall in blood pressure. Taking sildenafil with poppers (amyl nitrate) or illegal drugs such as amphetamines, ecstasy and cocaine can increase the risk of serious side effects.

The NHS asks people to tell a pharmacist or doctor about riociguat, heart medicines, epilepsy medicines, HIV medicines, antifungals and St John's wort. It also says it cannot confirm that herbal remedies and supplements are safe with sildenafil, because they are not tested in the same way as pharmacy and prescription medicines. UK product information says grapefruit juice is not recommended. The NHS says heavy drinking can make erections harder to get.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with sildenafil?
sections.body:
The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to sildenafil, nitrates taken for angina, low blood pressure and a recent stroke or heart attack among the reasons it may not be suitable. It also lists a rare inherited eye disease such as retinitis pigmentosa and a curved penis (Peyronie's disease).

A formulary note lists past sudden vision loss from reduced blood flow to the optic nerve as a reason to avoid it. For erection problems, the NHS says sildenafil is not usually used in pregnancy. The NHS says it does not usually cause sleepiness, but driving or cycling is not advised if it causes dizziness or blurred vision.

faqs.q: Can sildenafil be taken with nitrates for chest pain?
faqs.a: The NHS says it can be dangerous to take sildenafil with nitrates, which are often given for chest pain. The combination can cause a dangerous fall in blood pressure. The NHS says sildenafil is not usually prescribed with nitrates, so people who take GTN for chest pain ask a pharmacist or doctor for advice.

faqs.q: Are poppers a problem with sildenafil?
faqs.a: The NHS says taking sildenafil with poppers (amyl nitrate) or illegal drugs such as amphetamines, ecstasy and cocaine can increase the risk of serious side effects. UK product information says the nitrate warning also covers amyl nitrite.

faqs.q: Is long-term use harmful?
faqs.a: The NHS says sildenafil can be taken for a long time, with no lasting harmful effects seen over many months or years. Side effects such as headache and dizziness can still happen.

faqs.q: Do herbal versions of Viagra work?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no such thing as herbal Viagra, and products sold under that name may be fake or unsafe. It also says it cannot confirm that herbal remedies and supplements are safe with sildenafil.

faqs.q: What does the NHS say about a painful erection?
faqs.a: A painful erection that lasts a long time is listed as a serious side effect, and the advice is to call 999 or go to A&E. For a sudden decrease or loss of vision, the NHS says to stop taking sildenafil and call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away.

faqs.q: Can women take sildenafil?
faqs.a: The NHS says women can take sildenafil for pulmonary hypertension, but there is no good evidence that it helps sexual problems in women.

tadalafil.name: Tadalafil
tadalafil.summary: Tadalafil is a medicine mainly used to treat erection problems. The NHS says it is also sometimes prescribed for urinary problems linked to an enlarged prostate and for pulmonary arterial hypertension. The NHS says it is not usually taken with nitrates, and a painful or prolonged erection is a serious side effect for which hospital guidance advises 999 or A&E.
usedFor: Erection problems (erectile dysfunction), the main use the NHS names.
Urinary problems caused by an enlarged prostate (benign prostate enlargement).
Pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Second-line treatment for Raynaud's phenomenon and digital ulcers, according to one NHS hospital leaflet.
tadalafil.howItWorks: Tadalafil belongs to a group of medicines called PDE5 inhibitors. StatPearls describes these medicines as stopping the PDE5 enzyme from breaking down a chemical messenger called cGMP. UK patient leaflets say tadalafil does not cause an erection by itself, and sexual stimulation is still needed. StatPearls says its effect on the prostate and bladder helps relieve enlarged prostate symptoms by relaxing these tissues and improving urine flow.

The serious side effects the NHS lists include an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) with a swollen throat or tongue, a raised itchy rash or difficulty breathing.
NHS medicine pages for similar drugs, such as sildenafil, give 999 for swelling of the lips, mouth or throat or difficulty breathing.
A painful or prolonged erection is listed as serious; hospital guidance advises 999 or A&E.
Sudden changes in hearing or eyesight are listed as serious, and MedlinePlus advises calling a doctor right away.
Seizures, palpitations and chest pain are also listed as serious.

cautions: The NHS says tadalafil is not usually taken with nitrates, such as GTN for chest pain, and advises asking a pharmacist or doctor if you take them.
StatPearls describes the nitrate-related fall in blood pressure as potentially life-threatening.
Poppers (amyl nitrate) or illegal drugs such as amphetamines, ecstasy and cocaine can increase the risk of serious side effects.
The NHS advises avoiding grapefruit juice.
Alcohol can cause dizziness or light-headedness by lowering blood pressure.
The NHS says tadalafil may not be suitable after a serious reaction to it before or a recent heart attack or stroke.
Liver or kidney problems, certain blood cancers such as leukaemia, sickle cell anaemia and a curved or bent penis that makes erections painful or difficult are also listed.
Past vision loss in one eye from reduced blood flow to the optic nerve is listed too.
The NHS advises avoiding tadalafil in pregnancy and while breastfeeding.
Local NHS guidance lists uncontrolled high blood pressure as a reason for caution.
A review says alpha-blockers call for caution when used with PDE5 inhibitors.

sections.heading: What is tadalafil used for?
sections.body:
The NHS says tadalafil is mainly used to treat erection problems. It is also sometimes prescribed for urinary problems linked to an enlarged prostate (benign prostate enlargement), and for pulmonary arterial hypertension, which is high blood pressure in the blood vessels to the lungs. Brand names include Cialis, Cialis Together and Adcirca.

A hospital patient leaflet describes both sildenafil and tadalafil as second-line treatments for Raynaud's phenomenon and for digital ulcers, which are sores on the fingers and toes. The MHRA has reclassified Cialis Together tablets as a pharmacy medicine.

sections.heading: How does tadalafil work?
sections.body:
Tadalafil belongs to a group of medicines called PDE5 inhibitors. StatPearls says PDE5 inhibitors stop the PDE5 enzyme from breaking down cGMP, a chemical messenger. UK patient leaflets say tadalafil does not cause an erection by itself, and sexual stimulation is still needed.

StatPearls adds that tadalafil's effect on the prostate and bladder helps relieve symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia by relaxing these tissues and improving urine flow. UK patient leaflets say the medicine may still be effective up to 36 hours after taking the tablet.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of tadalafil?
sections.body:
The NHS lists indigestion, muscle aches, back pain, a blocked nose, a flushed face and headaches as common side effects.

The NHS says serious side effects are possible but most are rare, and to call NHS 111 if you think you are having a serious side effect. The serious side effects it lists include an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) with a swollen throat or tongue, a raised itchy rash or difficulty breathing, sudden changes in hearing or eyesight, a painful or prolonged erection, seizures, palpitations and chest pain. NHS medicine pages for similar drugs, such as sildenafil, give 999 for swelling of the lips, mouth or throat or difficulty breathing. For a painful or prolonged erection, hospital guidance advises 999 or A&E. MedlinePlus advises calling a doctor right away for a sudden loss of vision or hearing, which may come with ringing in the ears or dizziness.

sections.heading: Tadalafil with other medicines, drugs and alcohol
sections.body:
The NHS says tadalafil is not usually taken with nitrates, such as GTN for chest pain, and advises asking a pharmacist or doctor if you take them. StatPearls describes the nitrate-related low blood pressure as potentially life-threatening. UK product information says tadalafil makes the blood-pressure-lowering effect of nitrates stronger, so using them together is contraindicated.

The NHS says poppers (amyl nitrate) and illegal drugs such as amphetamines, ecstasy and cocaine can increase the risk of serious side effects. The NHS advises avoiding grapefruit juice. Alcohol can cause dizziness or light-headedness through lower blood pressure. An NHS Highland guideline says tadalafil and sildenafil are contraindicated with nitrates and nicorandil, and a review calls for caution with alpha-blockers.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with tadalafil?
sections.body:
The NHS says tadalafil may not be suitable for everyone. This includes people who have had a serious reaction to it before or who have recently had a heart attack or stroke. It also includes people with liver or kidney problems.

Blood cancers such as leukaemia and sickle cell anaemia are also listed. So are past vision loss in one eye from reduced blood flow to the optic nerve, and a curved or bent penis that makes erections painful or difficult. Local NHS guidance lists uncontrolled high blood pressure as a reason for caution. The NHS advises avoiding tadalafil in pregnancy and while breastfeeding.

faqs.q: Can tadalafil be taken with nitrates?
faqs.a: The NHS says tadalafil is not usually taken with nitrates, such as GTN for chest pain, and advises asking a pharmacist or doctor if you take them. StatPearls describes the nitrate-related fall in blood pressure as potentially life-threatening.

faqs.q: Are poppers or alcohol a problem with tadalafil?
faqs.a: The NHS says taking tadalafil with poppers (amyl nitrate) or illegal drugs such as amphetamines, ecstasy and cocaine can increase the risk of serious side effects. It advises avoiding grapefruit juice. Alcohol can cause dizziness or light-headedness because it lowers blood pressure.

faqs.q: Can tadalafil be used for prostate symptoms?
faqs.a: The NHS says tadalafil is sometimes prescribed for urinary problems linked to an enlarged prostate (benign prostate enlargement). StatPearls says its effect on the prostate and bladder helps relieve these symptoms by relaxing these tissues.

faqs.q: What does the NHS say about sudden vision or hearing changes?
faqs.a: The NHS lists sudden changes in hearing or eyesight as serious side effects of tadalafil. MedlinePlus says a sudden decrease or loss of vision or hearing is a reason to call a doctor right away. For sildenafil, the NHS gives a doctor or NHS 111 as the route for sudden loss of vision.

faqs.q: Can tadalafil be used in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS advises avoiding tadalafil in pregnancy and while breastfeeding.

faqs.q: What does a painful erection mean on tadalafil?
faqs.a: The NHS lists a painful or prolonged erection as a serious side effect. Hospital guidance advises calling 999 or going to A&E. The NHS lists seizures and chest pain among the other serious side effects.

combined-pill.name: Combined oral contraceptive pill
combined-pill.summary: The combined pill is a hormonal contraceptive that contains two hormones, oestrogen and a progestogen. It mainly works by stopping the ovaries releasing an egg. It carries a very small risk of blood clots; sudden breathlessness or chest pain needs a 999 call or A&E. Pain and swelling in one leg can be a clot, and the NHS advises getting medical help through an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.
usedFor: Contraception: preventing pregnancy, which the NHS says the combined pill does with over 99% effectiveness when always used perfectly
Making periods regular, lighter and less painful, which the NHS says it usually does
Easing the symptoms of premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and endometriosis, where the NHS says it may help
combined-pill.howItWorks: The combined pill contains two hormones, oestrogen and progestogen. It mainly works by stopping the ovaries releasing an egg each month. It also thickens the mucus made by the cervix, which makes it harder for sperm to pass.

common: Bleeding between periods or changes to periods are common in the first few months.
Headaches, mood changes, nausea and sore breasts are also listed.
The NHS says there is no evidence that the pill causes weight gain or changes sex drive.
serious: A blood clot in the leg or lung, a clot causing a heart attack, or a clot causing a stroke is a possible risk, which the NHS describes as very small.
For a possible clot in the lung, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden difficulty breathing, chest or upper back pain, a very fast heartbeat or fainting.

Coughing up blood is also listed as a symptom of a clot in the lung, and the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for coughing up more than a few spots or streaks of blood, or coughing up blood with difficulty breathing, a very fast heartbeat or chest pain.

Throbbing pain, usually in the calf or thigh, with swelling in one leg can be a clot in the leg, and the NHS advises getting medical help as soon as possible, for example through an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

The UK medicines regulator found that pills containing drospirenone, gestodene or desogestrel carry a higher relative risk of clots than those containing levonorgestrel, norethisterone or norgestimate.
Taking the pill can cause high blood pressure in a small number of people, which a GP can check.
The NHS says the pill can slightly increase the risk of breast and cervical cancer and can lower the risk of womb, ovarian and bowel cancer.

cautions: The pill is not suitable for everyone, and a clinician checks risk factors, including those for blood clots, before prescribing.
Conditions that may make it unsuitable include a history of blood clots, migraine with aura, breast cancer, liver cancer or severe cirrhosis, complications of diabetes and heart problems.
The NHS also lists obesity, and smoking at older ages, as reasons the pill may not suit someone.
Some medicines can make the pill less effective, including some used for TB, epilepsy or HIV, and the herbal remedy St John's wort.
The NHS names the antibiotics rifampicin and rifabutin as ones that can reduce its effectiveness.
It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections, so condoms are still needed for that.
combined-pill.monitoring: A clinician checks suitability and blood clot risk factors before prescribing. Blood pressure can rise in a small number of people. If side effects are still a problem after about three months, the NHS says to speak to a pharmacist or doctor, and a different pill may help.

sections.heading: What is the combined pill?
sections.body:
The combined pill is a hormonal contraceptive, often just called the pill. It contains two hormones, oestrogen and a progestogen. The emc lists UK brands as ethinylestradiol, an oestrogen, combined with a progestogen. Microgynon and Logynon contain levonorgestrel, Marvelon contains desogestrel, and Yasmin contains drospirenone.

The same two kinds of hormone are also given as a skin patch or a vaginal ring. The NHS says the pill is available from sexual health clinics, GP surgeries and young people's services. Some pharmacies can also supply it, without a prescription and free of charge, after a consultation with a pharmacist.

sections.heading: How does it work, and how well?
sections.body:
The pill mainly works by stopping the ovaries releasing an egg each month. It also makes the mucus from the cervix thicker, which makes it harder for sperm to pass. The NHS says the combined pill is more than 99% effective at preventing pregnancy when always used perfectly. Missed pills, vomiting or severe diarrhoea can make it less effective.

Some medicines and herbal remedies can also stop the pill working properly. The pill does not protect against sexually transmitted infections, so condoms are still needed for that.

sections.heading: What are the benefits and side effects?
sections.body:
The NHS says the pill usually makes periods regular, lighter and less painful, and that it may help with premenstrual syndrome and endometriosis. Bleeding between periods or changes to periods are common in the first few months. Headaches, mood changes, nausea and sore breasts are also listed.

The NHS says there is no evidence that the pill causes weight gain or changes sex drive. Taking the pill can cause high blood pressure in a small number of people. The NHS says the pill can slightly increase the risk of breast and cervical cancer and can lower the risk of womb, ovarian and bowel cancer. If side effects are still a problem after about three months, the NHS says to speak to a pharmacist or doctor, and a different pill may suit better.

sections.heading: Blood clots: what to know and where to go
sections.body:
The NHS lists the possible risks as a blood clot in the leg or lung, a clot causing a heart attack, or a clot causing a stroke. It describes the risk as very small, and a clinician checks risk factors before prescribing. The UK medicines regulator found that pills containing drospirenone, gestodene or desogestrel carry a higher relative risk than those containing levonorgestrel, norethisterone or norgestimate.

For a possible clot in the lung, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden difficulty breathing, chest or upper back pain, a very fast heartbeat or fainting. Chest pain that is worse on breathing in, and coughing up blood, are also listed as symptoms. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for coughing up more than a few spots or streaks of blood, or coughing up blood with breathing difficulty or chest pain. A clot in the leg can cause throbbing pain, usually in the calf or thigh, and swelling in one leg. The NHS advises getting medical help as soon as possible, for example through an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

sections.heading: Who may not be able to use it?
sections.body:
The NHS says the combined pill is not suitable for everyone. Its list of conditions that may make it unsuitable includes a history of blood clots, migraine with aura, breast cancer, liver cancer or severe cirrhosis, complications of diabetes and heart problems. It also lists obesity, and smoking at older ages.

Some medicines can make the pill less effective, including some used for TB, epilepsy or HIV, and St John's wort. The NHS names the antibiotics rifampicin and rifabutin.

faqs.q: Does the combined pill protect against sexually transmitted infections?
faqs.a: No, the NHS says the combined pill does not protect against sexually transmitted infections, so condoms are still needed for that. Sexually transmitted infections, or STIs, are infections that pass from person to person through sexual contact.

faqs.q: Can the combined pill be obtained without seeing a GP?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is available from sexual health clinics, GP surgeries and young people's services. Some pharmacies can supply it without a prescription and free of charge after a consultation with a pharmacist, though not every pharmacy offers this.

faqs.q: What are the warning signs of a blood clot?
faqs.a: A clot in the lung can cause sudden difficulty breathing, chest pain that is worse on breathing in, and coughing up blood. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden difficulty breathing, chest or upper back pain, a very fast heartbeat or fainting. A clot in the leg can cause throbbing pain, usually in the calf or thigh, and swelling in one leg, and the NHS advises getting medical help as soon as possible, for example through an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

faqs.q: Does the combined pill cause weight gain?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no evidence that taking the pill makes a person put on weight or changes sex drive. Headaches, mood changes, nausea and sore breasts are among the listed side effects. If side effects are still a problem after about three months, the NHS says to speak to a pharmacist or doctor, and changing pill may help.

faqs.q: Which medicines can stop the combined pill working?
faqs.a: The NHS says some antibiotics, such as rifampicin and rifabutin, can reduce its effectiveness. Medicines used for TB, epilepsy or HIV, and St John's wort, are also named as able to make the pill less effective.

faqs.q: Does the combined pill change the risk of cancer?
faqs.a: The NHS says the pill can slightly increase the risk of breast cancer and cervical cancer, and can lower the risk of womb, ovarian and bowel cancers. The NHS says the breast and cervical cancer risk goes back to normal about 10 years after stopping the pill.

aciclovir.name: Aciclovir
aciclovir.summary: Aciclovir is an antiviral medicine used for infections such as cold sores, shingles, chickenpox and genital herpes. The NHS says no medicine or treatment removes the herpes virus from the body completely.
usedFor: Cold sores
Shingles
Chickenpox
Genital herpes
Herpes simplex eye infections
Preventing these infections in some people with a weakened immune system
aciclovir.howItWorks: Aciclovir is an antiviral medicine. The NHS says aciclovir stops the herpes virus growing and spreading, which helps the immune system deal with the infection. MedlinePlus describes aciclovir as a synthetic nucleoside analogue antiviral that works by stopping the spread of the herpes virus in the body. The NHS says no medicine or treatment removes the herpes virus from the body completely.
aciclovir.onset: The NHS says people should start to feel better after taking or using aciclovir for a few days, and advises starting as soon as the first signs of infection appear.

sections.heading: What is aciclovir used for?
sections.body: Aciclovir is an antiviral medicine. The NHS says it is used to treat infections such as cold sores, shingles, chickenpox and genital herpes, as well as herpes simplex infections of the eye. It is sometimes used to prevent these infections in people with a weakened immune system. The NHS describes tablets, a liquid to swallow, an eye ointment, a cold sore cream and a genital herpes cream; injections are usually given only in hospital. The NHS says cold sore cream can be bought at most pharmacies and shops without a prescription. Children can usually use the cream or ointment, and may be prescribed tablets for chickenpox and shingles.

sections.heading: How does aciclovir work?
sections.body: The NHS says aciclovir stops the herpes virus growing and spreading, which helps the immune system deal with the infection. MedlinePlus describes aciclovir as a synthetic nucleoside analogue antiviral that works by stopping the spread of the herpes virus in the body. The NHS says no medicine or treatment removes the herpes virus from the body completely. MedlinePlus says acyclovir does not cure cold sores or genital herpes, does not prevent outbreaks of them and does not stop their spread to other people. The NHS says people should start to feel better after taking or using aciclovir for a few days, and advises starting as soon as the first signs of infection appear. The NHS advises avoiding kissing and oral sex while a person or their partner has a cold sore, until the sores have healed, to reduce the risk of passing on the infection.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of aciclovir?
sections.body: The NHS lists headache, dizziness or feeling faint, feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, stomach ache, rash, itching, tiredness, a high temperature and a skin reaction after exposure to light as common side effects, which are usually mild. The NHS says creams are less likely to cause side effects, though some people get mild burning or stinging that usually goes away quickly. For a side effect that bothers someone or does not go away, the NHS suggests speaking to a pharmacist or doctor. A serious allergic reaction, with signs such as sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue or struggling to breathe, needs a 999 call, according to the NHS. Liver problems, kidney problems and changes to blood cells are also listed as serious side effects; the NHS advises calling NHS 111 if someone using or recently using aciclovir thinks they may be having these.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with aciclovir?
sections.body: The NHS advises telling a doctor before use about kidney problems, being over 65, being pregnant or trying to get pregnant, or breastfeeding. UK product information lists allergy to aciclovir or valaciclovir as a reason the medicine is not used. UK patient leaflets say the doctor may adjust treatment for children, people over 65 and people with kidney problems. For people with a weakened immune system, such as HIV or AIDS or a bone marrow transplant, the NHS advises talking to a doctor about the best type of aciclovir. Aciclovir is cleared through the kidneys, so the prescriber may adjust treatment for people with kidney problems.

sections.heading: Aciclovir with other medicines and alcohol
sections.body: UK product information says cimetidine and probenecid can raise aciclovir levels in the blood, and that aciclovir may raise theophylline levels. The NHS says there is not enough information to show that herbal remedies or supplements are safe to take with aciclovir, and that they are not tested in the same way as pharmacy and prescription medicines. The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking aciclovir.

faqs.q: Does aciclovir cure cold sores or herpes?
faqs.a: The NHS says no medicine or treatment removes the herpes virus from the body completely. MedlinePlus says acyclovir does not cure cold sores or genital herpes, does not prevent outbreaks of them and does not stop their spread to other people. The NHS says aciclovir stops the herpes virus growing and spreading, which helps the immune system deal with the infection.

faqs.q: How soon does aciclovir start to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says people should start to feel better after taking or using aciclovir for a few days, and advises starting as soon as the first signs of infection appear.

faqs.q: Can aciclovir cream be bought without a prescription?
faqs.a: The NHS says aciclovir cold sore cream can be bought at most pharmacies and shops without a prescription. A pharmacist can advise whether it suits the infection in question.

faqs.q: Can people drink alcohol while using aciclovir?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking aciclovir. A pharmacist or GP can answer questions about an individual situation.

The NHS says there is not enough information to show that herbal remedies or supplements are safe to take with aciclovir, and that they are not tested in the same way as pharmacy and prescription medicines.

fluconazole.name: Fluconazole
fluconazole.summary: Fluconazole is an antifungal medicine used for thrush and other fungal infections. The NHS says fluconazole is not usually recommended in pregnancy but may be used if the benefits outweigh the risks. A pharmacist or doctor is asked before use in pregnancy.
usedFor: Thrush in men and women, including vaginal thrush
Balanitis (inflammation of the head of the penis)
Oral thrush
Cryptococcal meningitis, a fungal brain infection
Preventing fungal infections in people at high risk, such as those with HIV or a weakened immune system
fluconazole.howItWorks: Fluconazole is an antifungal medicine. The NHS says fluconazole kills the fungus causing the infection by making holes in the fungus's cell membrane so that the contents leak out. MedlinePlus describes fluconazole as slowing the growth of the fungi that cause infection. Azole antifungals block a step in the making of ergosterol, a main part of fungal cell membranes.
fluconazole.onset: The NHS says symptoms of vaginal thrush, balanitis or oral thrush should be better within a week, and that a serious fungal infection can take longer, 1 to 2 weeks, to work fully.

common: The NHS lists stomach pain or discomfort, diarrhoea, headache, feeling or being sick and rash as common side effects, with nausea and diarrhoea the most common.
Dizziness is uncommon; the NHS advises not driving or cycling until the feeling goes away.
The NHS says fluconazole is not likely to affect contraception, but vomiting or severe diarrhoea can mean contraceptive pills do not protect against pregnancy.
serious: A severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), another hypersensitivity reaction or a severe skin reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome needs a 999 call, according to the NHS.

Liver problems can show as itching, darker urine, pale stools or yellowing of the skin or eyes, which may be harder to see on black or brown skin; the NHS advises calling NHS 111 for any other serious side effect.

cautions: The NHS says fluconazole is not usually recommended in pregnancy but may be used if the benefits outweigh the risks.

The NHS advises contraception for anyone who could become pregnant while taking fluconazole and for a short time after stopping, because the medicine could harm a baby or increase the chance of miscarriage.

The NHS lists an allergic reaction or serious side effect from fluconazole or another antifungal, liver or kidney problems, heart problems including rhythm problems, abnormal potassium, calcium or magnesium levels, and porphyria (a rare blood condition) as reasons fluconazole may not be suitable.

For vaginal thrush or balanitis, the NHS says most adults and children aged 16 or over can take fluconazole, while younger children, and people 16 or over who need it for other conditions, can take it if a doctor prescribes it.

The NHS names pimozide, quetiapine, amisulpride, haloperidol, lithium, risperidone, escitalopram, venlafaxine, warfarin, dabigatran, clopidogrel and statins among medicines to discuss with a doctor before starting fluconazole.
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking fluconazole.
fluconazole.monitoring: UK product information says prothrombin time, a blood clotting test, should be carefully monitored in people taking warfarin-type anticoagulants with fluconazole.

sections.heading: What is fluconazole used for?
sections.body: Fluconazole is an antifungal medicine. The NHS says it is used to treat infections caused by different kinds of fungus. These include thrush in men and women, such as vaginal thrush, balanitis (inflammation of the head of the penis) and oral thrush, and a fungal brain infection called cryptococcal meningitis. It is also used to prevent fungal infections in people at high risk, such as those with HIV or a weakened immune system. The NHS says fluconazole is available on prescription and can also be bought from a pharmacy for vaginal thrush or balanitis. The NHS says pharmacy purchase covers vaginal thrush or balanitis; the brand names it gives include Azocan and Canesten Thrush Oral Capsules.

sections.heading: How does fluconazole work?
sections.body: The NHS says fluconazole kills the fungus causing the infection by making holes in the fungus's cell membrane so that the contents leak out. MedlinePlus describes fluconazole as slowing the growth of the fungi that cause infection. Azole antifungals block a step in the making of ergosterol, a main part of fungal cell membranes. The NHS says symptoms of vaginal thrush, balanitis or oral thrush should be better within a week, and that a serious fungal infection can take longer, 1 to 2 weeks, to work fully. The NHS advises seeing a doctor if symptoms of thrush are not better within the expected time. The NHS describes capsules or a liquid to swallow, and says the length of treatment depends on the kind of infection.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of fluconazole?

The NHS says fluconazole is not likely to affect contraception, but vomiting or severe diarrhoea can mean contraceptive pills do not protect against pregnancy. A severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), another hypersensitivity reaction or a severe skin reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome needs a 999 call, according to the NHS. Liver problems can show as itching, darker urine, pale stools or yellowing of the skin or eyes, which may be harder to see on black or brown skin; the NHS advises calling NHS 111 for any other serious side effect.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with fluconazole?
sections.body: The NHS lists an allergic reaction or serious side effect from fluconazole or another antifungal, liver or kidney problems, heart problems including rhythm problems, abnormal potassium, calcium or magnesium levels, and porphyria (a rare blood condition) as reasons fluconazole may not be suitable. For vaginal thrush or balanitis, the NHS says most adults and children aged 16 or over can take fluconazole, while younger children, and people 16 or over who need it for other conditions, can take it if a doctor prescribes it. The NHS says fluconazole is not usually recommended in pregnancy but may be used if the benefits outweigh the risks. The NHS advises contraception for anyone who could become pregnant while taking fluconazole and for a short time after stopping, because the medicine could harm a baby or increase the chance of miscarriage. UK product information says prothrombin time, a blood clotting test, should be carefully monitored in people taking warfarin-type anticoagulants with fluconazole.

sections.heading: Fluconazole with other medicines and alcohol
sections.body: The NHS names pimozide, quetiapine, amisulpride, haloperidol, lithium, risperidone, escitalopram, venlafaxine, warfarin, dabigatran, clopidogrel and statins among medicines to discuss with a doctor before starting fluconazole. A pharmacist or doctor can say whether a particular combination causes problems. The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking fluconazole.

faqs.q: Can fluconazole be taken in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says fluconazole is not usually recommended in pregnancy but may be used if the benefits outweigh the risks. Anyone who is pregnant or might be pregnant is asked to speak to a pharmacist or doctor first.

faqs.q: Can fluconazole be bought from a pharmacy?
faqs.a: The NHS says fluconazole is available on prescription and can also be bought from a pharmacy for vaginal thrush or balanitis. For vaginal thrush or balanitis, the NHS says most adults and children aged 16 or over can take fluconazole, while younger children, and people 16 or over who need it for other conditions, can take it if a doctor prescribes it.

faqs.q: How long does fluconazole take to work for thrush?
faqs.a: The NHS says symptoms of vaginal thrush, balanitis or oral thrush should be better within a week, and that a serious fungal infection can take longer, 1 to 2 weeks, to work fully.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk during fluconazole treatment?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking fluconazole. Dizziness is uncommon; the NHS advises not driving or cycling until the feeling goes away.

faqs.q: Does fluconazole affect the contraceptive pill?
faqs.a: The NHS says fluconazole is not likely to affect contraception, but vomiting or severe diarrhoea can mean contraceptive pills do not protect against pregnancy. montelukast.name: Montelukast
montelukast.summary: Montelukast is a prescription medicine that helps prevent asthma symptoms. The MHRA warns that montelukast can cause neuropsychiatric reactions, including sleep disorders, hallucinations and changes in behaviour and mood. The MHRA advises patients to speak to their prescriber immediately, or seek urgent medical attention, if these reactions occur.
usedFor: Helping prevent asthma symptoms, usually as an add-on to a regular preventer inhaler
Asthma triggered by exercise or by seasonal allergies
Easing seasonal allergy symptoms such as hay fever

StatPearls describes it as blocking leukotriene effects such as airway swelling and smooth muscle contraction, without any stimulating action of its own. StatPearls says eosinophils are the main source of cysteinyl leukotrienes, which are important in recruiting more eosinophils.

common: Common side effects listed by the NHS include diarrhoea, a raised temperature, headaches, stomach pain, feeling or being sick and a mild rash.
The NHS gives self-care advice for these, such as fluids and rest, and says a pharmacist can advise.
Asthma and Lung UK says montelukast has been linked to depression and anxiety and describes mental health side effects as rare but serious.
serious: The NHS lists mood changes, hallucinations, sleep problems, speech changes such as stuttering and shaking or trembling among serious side effects.
An unusual or fast heartbeat, and yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes, which can be a sign of liver problems, are also listed.
For mood changes such as becoming anxious, depressed or aggressive, the NHS advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111 immediately.
The NHS says to call 999 for swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or difficulty breathing, which can signal a serious allergic reaction.
The MHRA advises patients to speak to their prescriber immediately, or seek urgent medical attention, if these reactions occur.
Asthma and Lung UK lists thoughts of suicide or self-harm as a very rare side effect.
Asthma and Lung UK advises talking to a GP or asthma nurse as soon as possible if montelukast affects sleep or mood.
For thoughts of suicide or self-harm, the usual routes are 999 if in immediate danger, NHS 111 (mental health option) or Samaritans on 116 123, free at any time.

cautions: The MHRA warns that montelukast can cause neuropsychiatric reactions, including sleep disorders, hallucinations and changes in behaviour and mood.
Prescribers are advised to stop montelukast if new or worsening neuropsychiatric symptoms appear.
The NHS asks anyone who has had an allergic reaction to montelukast or another medicine to tell the doctor.
The NHS lists epilepsy medicines such as phenobarbital or phenytoin, rifampicin and gemfibrozil as medicines to mention to a doctor or pharmacist before taking montelukast.

sections.heading: What is montelukast and how does it work?
sections.body:
Montelukast is a prescription medicine that helps prevent asthma symptoms. Asthma and Lung UK describes montelukast as an add-on taken alongside the regular preventer inhaler, and the NHS says it is usually prescribed when asthma is mild. The NHS says montelukast is not a rescue treatment and a reliever inhaler is used for an asthma attack. The NHS advises speaking to a doctor before stopping montelukast, because symptoms may return. The NHS and Asthma and Lung UK say it is also used when exercise or seasonal allergies trigger breathing difficulties. Asthma and Lung UK says it can improve symptoms of seasonal allergies such as hay fever. The NHS says most adults and children aged 6 months and over can take montelukast. The NHS describes tablets, chewable tablets and granules taken by mouth.

Asthma and Lung UK describes montelukast as working in a different way from steroid preventer inhalers. Montelukast blocks cysteinyl leukotriene type 1 receptors, which respond to leukotrienes. StatPearls describes it as blocking leukotriene effects such as airway swelling and smooth muscle contraction, without any stimulating action of its own. StatPearls says eosinophils are the main source of cysteinyl leukotrienes, which are important in recruiting more eosinophils.

sections.heading: Side effects
sections.body: Common side effects listed by the NHS include diarrhoea, a raised temperature, headaches, stomach pain, feeling or being sick and a mild rash. The NHS gives self-care advice for these, such as fluids and rest, and says a pharmacist can advise. Asthma and Lung UK says montelukast has been linked to depression and anxiety and describes mental health side effects as rare but serious. The NHS lists mood changes, hallucinations, sleep problems, speech changes such as stuttering and shaking or trembling among serious side effects. An unusual or fast heartbeat, and yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes, which can be a sign of liver problems, are also listed. For mood changes such as becoming anxious, depressed or aggressive, the NHS advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111 immediately. The NHS says to call 999 for swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or difficulty breathing, which can signal a serious allergic reaction.

sections.heading: Mood, behaviour and sleep: the MHRA warning
sections.body:
The MHRA warns that montelukast can cause neuropsychiatric reactions, including sleep disorders, hallucinations and changes in behaviour and mood. After a review, the MHRA said the risk is unchanged but is probably not well known to healthcare professionals, patients and carers, judging by Yellow Card reports. It said more prominent warnings would be added to the leaflet supplied with every pack, and its April 2024 Drug Safety Update says the warnings in the patient leaflet and product information have been strengthened and highlighted with a black box. The MHRA advises patients to speak to their prescriber immediately, or seek urgent medical attention, if these reactions occur. Prescribers are advised to stop montelukast if new or worsening neuropsychiatric symptoms appear. The MHRA encourages patients, carers and healthcare professionals to report suspected side effects to the Yellow Card scheme.

Asthma and Lung UK advises talking to a GP or asthma nurse as soon as possible if montelukast affects sleep or mood. Asthma and Lung UK lists thoughts of suicide or self-harm as a very rare side effect. For thoughts of suicide or self-harm, the usual routes are 999 if in immediate danger, NHS 111 (mental health option) or Samaritans on 116 123, free at any time.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, other medicines and who needs care
sections.body: The NHS says montelukast can be taken in pregnancy, that it is important asthma is well controlled, and that a doctor should be told if pregnancy happens, as they may review the medicine. The NHS says breastfeeding is possible if a doctor, health visitor or midwife says the baby is healthy; montelukast passes into breast milk in tiny amounts and has not been known to cause side effects in breastfed babies. The NHS asks anyone who has had an allergic reaction to montelukast or another medicine to tell the doctor. The NHS lists epilepsy medicines such as phenobarbital or phenytoin, rifampicin and gemfibrozil as medicines to mention to a doctor or pharmacist before taking montelukast. UK product information says some of these can change montelukast levels.

faqs.q: Can montelukast affect mood and behaviour?
faqs.a: The MHRA warns that montelukast can cause neuropsychiatric reactions, including sleep disorders, hallucinations and changes in behaviour and mood. After a review, the MHRA said the risk is unchanged but is probably not well known to healthcare professionals, patients and carers, judging by Yellow Card reports. The MHRA advises patients to speak to their prescriber immediately, or seek urgent medical attention, if these reactions occur.

faqs.q: Can montelukast be used for an asthma attack?
faqs.a: The NHS says montelukast is not a rescue treatment and a reliever inhaler is used for an asthma attack. The NHS advises speaking to a doctor before stopping montelukast, because symptoms may return.

The NHS says breastfeeding is possible if a doctor, health visitor or midwife says the baby is healthy; montelukast passes into breast milk in tiny amounts and has not been known to cause side effects in breastfed babies.

faqs.a: Montelukast is a prescription medicine that helps prevent asthma symptoms. The NHS and Asthma and Lung UK say it is also used when exercise or seasonal allergies trigger breathing difficulties. Asthma and Lung UK says it can improve symptoms of seasonal allergies such as hay fever.

faqs.q: What happens if mood or sleep changes appear?
faqs.a: The MHRA advises patients to speak to their prescriber immediately, or seek urgent medical attention, if these reactions occur. For mood changes such as becoming anxious, depressed or aggressive, the NHS advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111 immediately. Asthma and Lung UK advises talking to a GP or asthma nurse as soon as possible if montelukast affects sleep or mood. The MHRA encourages patients, carers and healthcare professionals to report suspected side effects to the Yellow Card scheme.

pde5-inhibitors.name: PDE5 inhibitors
pde5-inhibitors.summary: PDE5 inhibitors are medicines that include sildenafil and tadalafil, used mainly for erection problems. Some are also used for pulmonary hypertension. The NHS warns against combining them with nitrates and poppers because blood pressure can fall sharply.
pde5-inhibitors.mechanism: StatPearls says these drugs stop the PDE5 enzyme from breaking down cGMP, a chemical messenger. StatPearls also says nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors both cause blood vessels to widen, so using them together can cause severe low blood pressure.
classEffects: Headache, indigestion and a blocked nose are among the side effects the NHS lists for sildenafil and tadalafil.
A painful or prolonged erection and sudden changes in sight or hearing are listed as serious.
cautions: StatPearls says combining PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates is contraindicated because of the risk of profound and potentially life-threatening low blood pressure.
The NHS lists poppers and some illegal drugs as raising the risk of serious side effects.
A recent heart attack or stroke is among the reasons the NHS lists against use of sildenafil and tadalafil.
A review says alpha-blockers call for caution with PDE5 inhibitors.

combined-hormonal-contraceptives.name: Combined hormonal contraceptives
combined-hormonal-contraceptives.summary: Combined hormonal contraceptives contain both an oestrogen and a progestogen, and include the combined pill, a skin patch and a vaginal ring.
combined-hormonal-contraceptives.mechanism: They work mainly by stopping ovulation, the release of an egg from the ovaries. For the combined pill, NHS sources add that the mucus made by the cervix becomes thicker.
cautions: They carry a risk of blood clots in the leg or lung, heart attack and stroke, which the NHS describes as very small.
The UK medicines regulator found a higher relative risk of clots with drospirenone, gestodene and desogestrel products than with levonorgestrel, norethisterone or norgestimate products.
A history of blood clots, migraine with aura, breast cancer, liver cancer or severe cirrhosis, heart problems or complications of diabetes can make the combined pill unsuitable.
Some medicines, including some for TB, epilepsy or HIV and the herbal remedy St John's wort, can make the combined pill less effective.
The NHS notes that some hormonal contraceptives can change the effect of other medicines, such as the epilepsy treatment lamotrigine.

classWarnings.text: Blood clots: for a possible clot in the lung, sudden difficulty breathing, chest or upper back pain, a very fast heartbeat or fainting needs a 999 call or A&E; for a possible clot in the leg, the NHS advises getting medical help as soon as possible, for example an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.
The combined pill does not protect against sexually transmitted infections.

nucleoside-antivirals.name: Nucleoside antivirals
nucleoside-antivirals.summary: Antiviral medicines used for herpes virus infections such as cold sores, shingles, chickenpox and genital herpes. Aciclovir is described on this site, and valaciclovir is a related medicine.
nucleoside-antivirals.mechanism: MedlinePlus describes aciclovir as a synthetic nucleoside analogue antiviral that works by stopping the spread of the herpes virus in the body. The NHS says aciclovir stops the herpes virus growing and spreading, which helps the immune system deal with the infection. The NHS says no medicine or treatment removes the herpes virus from the body completely. NIH LiverTox describes valaciclovir as a nucleoside analogue antiviral and a prodrug of aciclovir.
cautions: UK product information lists allergy to aciclovir or valaciclovir as a reason the medicine is not used.
UK product information says aciclovir is cleared through the kidneys, so treatment may be adjusted in kidney problems.

classInteractions.effect: UK product information says these can raise aciclovir levels in the blood.

classInteractions.effect: UK product information says aciclovir may raise theophylline levels.

source.title: emc: Aciclovir 400 mg Tablets summary of product characteristics

classWarnings.text: A serious allergic reaction, with signs such as sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue or struggling to breathe, needs a 999 call, according to the NHS.

Liver problems, kidney problems and changes to blood cells are also listed as serious side effects; the NHS advises calling NHS 111 if someone using or recently using aciclovir thinks they may be having these.

azole-antifungals.name: Azole antifungals
azole-antifungals.summary: Antifungal medicines, including fluconazole, used for thrush and other fungal infections.
azole-antifungals.mechanism: Azole antifungals block a step in the making of ergosterol, a main part of fungal cell membranes. The NHS says fluconazole kills the fungus causing the infection by making holes in the fungus's cell membrane so that the contents leak out. MedlinePlus describes fluconazole as slowing the growth of the fungi that cause infection.
cautions: The NHS lists an allergic reaction or serious side effect from fluconazole or another antifungal, liver or kidney problems, heart problems including rhythm problems, abnormal potassium, calcium or magnesium levels, and porphyria (a rare blood condition) as reasons fluconazole may not be suitable.
The NHS says fluconazole is not usually recommended in pregnancy but may be used if the benefits outweigh the risks.

classInteractions.with: Pimozide, quetiapine, amisulpride, haloperidol, lithium, risperidone, escitalopram, venlafaxine, warfarin, dabigatran, clopidogrel, statins (with fluconazole)
classInteractions.effect: The NHS names these among medicines to discuss with a doctor before starting fluconazole.

classWarnings.text: A severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), another hypersensitivity reaction or a severe skin reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome needs a 999 call, according to the NHS.

Liver problems can show as itching, darker urine, pale stools or yellowing of the skin or eyes, which may be harder to see on black or brown skin; the NHS advises calling NHS 111 for any other serious side effect.

leukotriene-receptor-antagonists.name: Leukotriene receptor antagonists
leukotriene-receptor-antagonists.summary: Montelukast is a prescription medicine that helps prevent asthma symptoms. Asthma and Lung UK describes it as an add-on taken alongside the regular preventer inhaler.
leukotriene-receptor-antagonists.mechanism: Montelukast and zafirlukast block cysteinyl leukotriene type 1 receptors but not type 2 receptors. StatPearls says eosinophils are the main source of cysteinyl leukotrienes, which are important in recruiting more eosinophils.
cautions: The MHRA warns that montelukast can cause neuropsychiatric reactions, including sleep disorders, hallucinations and changes in behaviour and mood.
The MHRA advises patients to speak to their prescriber immediately, or seek urgent medical attention, if these reactions occur.

classInteractions.with: Some epilepsy medicines, rifampicin and gemfibrozil
classInteractions.effect: The NHS lists epilepsy medicines such as phenobarbital or phenytoin, rifampicin and gemfibrozil as medicines to mention to a doctor or pharmacist before taking montelukast.
